title: Poverty rises to 16% as real household incomes fall below 2019 levels | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 6 November 2026 00:00
-     - 62

Poverty has reversed a decade of decline and real household incomes have fallen below their 2019 level, according to preliminary official data that underline how far price growth has outrun earnings.

The Department of Census and Statistics (DCS) put the poverty headcount index at 16% in the first quarter of 2025, against 14.3% in 2019, in a bulletin published in October, 2026 under the Finance, Planning and Economic Development Ministry. The rate had fallen steadily from 22.5% in 2012/13 before the reversal.

Real mean household income dropped 7.8% from 2019 to Rs. 65,969 at 2016 prices, and real median income dropped 11.1% to Rs. 41,623, the sharper fall falling on the household at the midpoint of the distribution. Nominal mean income rose 93.2% over the period to Rs. 120,266 and nominal median income 74.4% to Rs. 75,882, but the purchasing power of both declined.

The data place 3,419,069 people below the poverty line, a threshold set at Rs. 16,417 per person a month, against Rs. 6,966 in 2019. Of the total, 2,934,392 are rural, 279,054 urban and 205,624 on estates, where the incidence is highest at 23.0% against 17.3% in rural areas and 7.8% in towns.

Income remains heavily skewed. The poorest 20% of households averaged Rs. 22,612 a month against Rs. 335,679 for the richest 20%, a gap of nearly 15 times. Urban households averaged Rs. 178,455 against Rs. 110,613 in rural areas and Rs. 72,558 on estates, while mean household size was 3.4.

Mean monthly expenditure of Rs. 116,191 left an average margin of about Rs. 4,000 over income, though the median household spent Rs. 94,057 against median income of Rs. 75,882. Real mean expenditure rose to Rs. 63,734 from Rs. 55,430 in 2019, and real median expenditure to Rs. 51,593 from Rs. 41,745.

The DCS cautioned that the estimates are provisional, rest on the first-quarter sample of the 25,000 households surveyed from January to December 2025 and are provided only to sector level pending final validation. Sampling variability is highest for the urban and estate figures, with coefficients of variation of 18.0% and 18.8% on the poverty index.

The survey, the eleventh in the series, was last conducted in 2019 and was planned for 2022 before being deferred to follow the Population and Housing Census completed in 2024. The full-year report will carry district-level estimates.

title: No additional burden: Govt. explains recent tax measures | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 6 November 2026 00:36
-     - 166

Finance Deputy Minister 

Dr. Anil Jayantha Fernando

The Government has not added to the public’s tax burden and has instead moved to correct flaws in an unfair tax structure, Deputy Finance Minister Dr. Anil Jayantha Fernando said, rejecting claims by Opposition groups circulating on social media over eight recent measures.

In a statement on Wednesday, Dr. Fernando said tax revenue is the primary source of funding for education, healthcare, development activity and infrastructure, and that the Government had spent two years improving collection efficiency, tax administration and public compliance. The tax base has since widened, allowing the Government to collect more revenue in 2025 than budgeted, he said.

He described the recent claims as misleading and said they amounted to a ‘distortion of facts’.

On the 6% increase in excise duty applied in January 2025, Dr. Fernando said the change was not a new tax but an adjustment under the existing indexation mechanism, which revises rates on selected goods by adding 4 percentage points to the previous year’s average inflation rate. Based on 2024 inflation, the formula produced a 6% revision. A 14% increase was applied under the same mechanism in 2024, during the administration of Ranil Wickremesinghe.

The Government has since declined to apply the 2026 revision, exercising flexibility built into the formula, citing the economic shock caused by Cyclone Ditwah.

Dr. Fernando said revisions to customs duty on electric vehicles formed part of a restructuring of the existing tariff regime rather than an additional levy, aimed at correcting shortcomings in the structure and curbing revenue losses.

The 50% surcharge on customs duty for private vehicle imports followed pressure on the foreign exchange market and higher dollar demand arising from the conflict in the Middle East. Rather than restricting imports across the board, the Government opted for the surcharge as a short-term measure to manage outflows. He said the objective was to protect reserves and prevent shortages of essential goods, not to raise revenue.

On withholding tax, the rate deducted at source from interest income rose to 10% from 5%. Dr. Fernando said the previous arrangement had penalised people outside the income tax net, few of whom pursued refunds. Such individuals can now obtain exemption by submitting a declaration or affidavit confirming their tax-exempt status, while the 10% deducted from those liable to income tax is credited against their final assessment.

He said the corporate tax rate on alcohol and tobacco companies rose to 45% from 40% because the sectors carry a greater capacity to generate profit, describing them as ‘sin industries’ in international usage.

On service exports, Dr. Fernando said exporters of services had been shielded by exemptions and interpretations under the former tax laws, leaving an imbalance against goods exporters and domestic service providers. Service exporters have been brought into the tax net at 15% for companies, against the 30% rate proposed by the previous Government, with individuals capped at 15% instead of rates of up to 36%.

He said VAT on services supplied through digital platforms, such as ride-hailing and food delivery applications, was intended to equalise treatment with operators delivering the same services conventionally.

The 20.5% rate on financial services consolidates VAT at 18% and the Social Security Contribution Levy (SSCL) at 2.5%, both previously calculated on the same base but administered under separate documentation and procedures.

Dr. Fernando said rate changes alone were an insufficient gauge of the overall burden.

“Changes in tax rates alone should not be used as the basis for determining whether the overall tax burden has increased.”

“Attention must also be paid to fairness in the tax system, adherence to policy principles, the proper utilisation of tax revenue, and measures to prevent waste, fraud and corruption.”

He said supply of fuel, fertiliser and medicines had continued without interruption through the Middle East conflict, crediting the Government’s economic management.

The Minister’s defence rests on a revenue base that has widened quickly but is still collected weakly. Revenue has doubled to 15.4% of GDP since 2021, from 7.3%, yet VAT non-filing rose to 19.1% among non-large taxpayers and 4% among large ones between 2025 and the first quarter of 2026, while income tax non-filing reached 52.7% for corporate income tax and 67.8% for individual income tax in 2025. Tax defaults reached about Rs. 2.1 trillion at 31 December, 2025, with about Rs. 1.6 trillion under dispute.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has said the next phase turns on compliance rather than rates. In a diagnostic published by the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development on 30 October, 2026, its Fiscal Affairs Department said risk-based methods were not yet embedded in daily operations and that penalties available in law were applied inconsistently.

“In Sri Lanka’s case, the Medium Term Revenue Strategy (MTRS) should be seen less as a vehicle for short-term tightening and more as a platform for locking in recent gains,” the report said. It put the yield from lifting revenue administration capability to 0.55 from 0.39 on its Operational Strength Index at about 1.9 percentage points of GDP over five years, an illustrative figure, and warned that the maintenance contract for the Inland Revenue Department’s core filing and payment platform expires on 31 January, 2027 (see: https://www.ft.lk/front-page/With-gains-exhausted-Govt-must-overhaul-tax-administration-IMF/44-799541).

Investors read the fiscal position more generously. Capital Alliance Holdings PLC (CAL) Group CEO Kanishke Mannakkara told a media briefing this week that the fiscal responsibility framework must continue through the upcoming Budget and called the widening of the tax net ‘very laudable efforts’. 

“The primary headwinds for Sri Lanka right now are external and geopolitical rather than structural domestic issues. Once tensions in the Middle East subside, I expect Sri Lanka and neighbouring regional markets to regain upward momentum,” Singapore-based Asia Frontier Capital Fund Manager Ruchir Desai said (see: https://www.ft.lk/front-page/SL-fundamentals-strong-for-frontier-revival--Budget-must-focus-on-fiscal-reforms-momentum/44-799571).

title: IRD kicks the TIN down the road | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 6 November 2026 00:24
-     - 85

The Inland Revenue Department (IRD) has postponed the compulsory production of Taxpayer Identification Numbers (TIN) for eight transactions until 1 April, 2027, five months after the requirement took effect, after applicants struggled to obtain the numbers.

The Commissioner General of Inland Revenue confirmed the decision, extending the deadline from 1 November, 2026.

The department said the requirement would now apply to opening bank accounts, obtaining building plan approvals, registering vehicles, renewing vehicle revenue licences, registering land, registering businesses, transferring company shares and obtaining credit cards from 1 April, 2027.

The postponement follows long queues at IRD offices and outages in the online registration system, which left applicants unable to secure a number in time to complete the listed transactions.

The Government had earlier granted temporary relief confined to bank account openings and vehicle revenue licence renewals.

The IRD is midway through a taxpayer register cleanup backed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which found in a diagnostic published on 30 October, 2026 that the department’s core platform for registration, filing and payment faces the expiry of its maintenance contract on 31 January, 2027.

title: Sri Lankan blue swimming crab fishery achieves MSC certification following decade of collaboration | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 6 November 2026 00:23
-     - 60

BSC fisherman stepping ashore after a day’s fishing – Pic by Opmeer Reports

The North-Western Sri Lanka blue swimming crab fishery has become the country’s first to achieve Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification, meeting the internationally recognised MSC Fisheries Standard for environmental sustainability in fishing. 

The milestone follows more than a decade of collaboration between fishing communities, seafood exporters, Government authorities and other stakeholders to strengthen fisheries management and support the long-term sustainability of the country’s blue swimming crab stocks.

The certification covers blue swimming crab (Portunus pelagicus) fishing in two areas off Sri Lanka’s north-western coast: Palk Bay and the Gulf of Mannar. Small-scale fishers use bottom-set gillnets from traditional boats and small motorised vessels, supplying international seafood markets across North America and Europe.

The journey towards certification began in 2013, when the Seafood Exporters’ Association of Sri Lanka, with support from the National Fisheries Institute Crab Council, brought together stakeholders to improve scientific understanding of crab stocks, assess fishing impacts on marine habitats and strengthen fisheries management.

Over the past decade, improved data collection has enhanced scientific stock assessments and informed the development of harvest strategies and fishery management plans. The fishery has also introduced measures to minimise impacts on non-target species and vulnerable marine life, and to protect juvenile crabs through a minimum legal purchasing size of 100 grams (≈ 117 mm).

Sri Lanka Blue Swimming Crab Fishery Improvement Project (FIP) Coordinator and Pelagikos Ltd., Executive Director Dr. Steve Creech said: “The success of the fishery improvement project in achieving MSC certification is built on a three-way partnership that promotes responsible harvesting by fishers, responsible purchasing by the seafood supply chain and collaborative fisheries management by the Department of Fisheries.

“Central to this approach has been the continuous collection and analysis of data on crab stocks and ecological impacts, and fisheries management. The scientific evidence gathered by pelagikos in collaboration with FIP members has been instrumental in enabling the two units of assessment (UoAs) to meet the MSC’s Standard.”

MSC certification is an important milestone for the coastal communities that depend on the fishery for their livelihoods. The sector supports thousands of small-scale fishers and a wider supply chain of collection centres and labour-intensive processing facilities, which employ thousands of women in preparing crab meat for export.

Representing the client group Taprobane Seafoods Ltd., Co-Founder and Managing Director Timothy O’Reilly said: “It’s remarkable to reflect that we began this journey shortly after the end of Sri Lanka’s 30-year civil conflict. Years of dedication and collaboration have brought us to this important milestone for the fishing communities we work with and Sri Lanka’s blue swimming crab industry.”

“With leading global retailers committed to sourcing seafood from fisheries certified to the MSC Fisheries Standard, we now have an exciting opportunity to share our story, build new partnerships and supply regional and global markets with responsibly sourced Sri Lankan blue swimming crab carrying the MSC ecolabel.”

CM Blue Crab Ltd., and co-client on the MSC certificate Director John D. Paterson said: “When we established our processing facility in Mannar in 2016, we invested in the long-term future of the fishery and its communities. MSC certification reflects years of dedicated collaboration to protect crab stocks while creating lasting livelihood opportunities for families in Mannar and Jaffna, and connecting local seafood production to international markets.”

Sri Lanka’s Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources Director General Susantha Kahawatte said: “The MSC certification of Sri Lanka’s blue swimming crab stocks mark an important milestone in our commitment to sustainable fisheries management through science-based decision-making, responsible fishing practices and collaboration between Government, industry and coastal communities.

“This achievement supports the conservation of marine resources, safeguards fishing livelihoods and strengthens Sri Lanka’s position in international seafood markets. MSC certification demonstrates our commitment to the long-term sustainability and competitiveness of the fisheries sector.”

MSC’s Regional Director Edouard le Bart said: “We congratulate everyone involved in this significant achievement and welcome the addition of Sri Lankan blue swimming crab to the global supply of MSC certified seafood, helping to meet growing market demand for sustainably sourced crab.”

“Sri Lanka’s dedication and experience also offer valuable lessons for other fisheries pursuing improvements, including the blue swimming crab FIPs in neighbouring India, Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam and Philippines. Sharing knowledge and strengthening regional cooperation can help advance sustainable fisheries management across shared marine ecosystems.”

With this certification, Sri Lanka’s blue swimming crab join a growing global network of certified fisheries, strengthening the country’s position as a supplier of responsibly sourced seafood to international markets.

title: Strong 2Q lifts Hemas 1H revenue to Rs. 67 b, up 9.5% | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 6 November 2026 00:21
-     - 99

Hemas Holdings PLC yesterday said it delivered a strong second quarter, with revenue growing 17% year-on-year (YoY) to Rs. 37.8 billion as all four sectors recorded growth, led by hospitals (+19.3%) and consumer brands

(+18.3%). 

EBITDA rebounded to Rs. 4.5 billion, up 10.5% YoY and nearly double the first quarter. Group earnings more than doubled from 1Q to Rs. 2 billion. For 1H FY27, the strong second quarter turned a 14.1% EBITDA decline at the end of 1Q into growth of 0.9%, with revenue growing 9.5% YoY to Rs. 67 billion.

During 1H, the Consumer Brands segments reported a revenue of Rs. 24.7 billion, up 13.4% from a year ago while earnings fell 30% to Rs. 1.6 billion. Life Sciences posted revenue of Rs, 34.5 billion, up 6% from a year ago with earnings falling 24% to Rs. 1.3 billion. Hospitals saw revenue grew 15% to Rs. 6.2 billion in 1H with earnings up 15% to Rs. 515 million. The Mobility segment saw revenue grow 10% YoY to Rs. 1.2 billion with earnings surging 58% to 627 million.

The Group chose to absorb much of the increase in raw material, energy and freight costs driven by the Middle East conflict, protecting consumer affordability and volumes. Gross margin declined 3.1pp YoY to 29.7%; however, disciplined cost management kept overheads growing slower than revenue, enabling EBITDA growth. Higher finance costs, reflecting increased borrowings to fund working capital and the Twiga acquisition, together with a higher tax charge, resulted in Group earnings declining 3% YoY, the company said.

Within Consumer Brands, Beauty, Home Care and Baby Care all delivered double-digit growth, with Beauty now accounting for 20% of the home and personal care portfolio. In Bangladesh, revenue recorded single-digit growth despite a challenging macroeconomic environment, with male grooming category growing by nearly 50%.

In Learning, newer adjacencies continued to gain traction, with Back-to-School and Bags volumes growing over 50% YoY. In Life Sciences, Hemas Pharmaceuticals retained its market leadership and secured six new product registrations during the quarter, while absorbing higher costs pending approval of regulated price revisions, and Morison’s own-brand volumes grew 23% YoY.

During the quarter, Hemas completed its first international acquisition, a 75% stake in Twiga Stationers and Printers Limited, a leading stationery manufacturer and exporter in East Africa. Revenue is tracking in line with projections, and Twiga provides a platform for long-term growth across the region.

Looking ahead, price revisions in pharmaceuticals, ongoing cost and productivity initiatives, and the third stage of the public sector salary revision in 2027 are expected to support margins and volumes. Hemas remains focused on its Long Range Plan targets of mid-teen compound annual growth in revenue and earnings, with 15% of revenue to be derived from international markets by FY30, and has earmarked over $ 100 million for new growth platforms, to be deployed with discipline.

Group CEO Ashish Chandra said: “2Q FY27 demonstrated the resilience of Hemas in a challenging environment. In a period shaped by the Middle East war, higher energy costs and a volatile currency, our teams protected consumers, ensured the continued availability of medicines and delivered a strong recovery in profitability from the first quarter. This resilience is the foundation on which we are building our next chapter.

“Our Long Range Plan sets clear north stars: mid-teen compound annual growth in both revenue and earnings, with 15% of revenue to be derived from international markets by FY30. To achieve this, we have earmarked over $ 100 million for new growth platforms. We will deploy this capital with discipline, prioritising opportunities that build on our strengths, offer scalable growth and meet clear return thresholds.

“Twiga represents our next step on the international journey. As it enters its school season, our priority is to deliver Twiga’s plan and develop it into a platform for growth across East Africa, reducing our dependence on a single economy and extending our learning expertise to many more young learners.

“In Sri Lanka, we expect the third stage of the public sector salary revision, amounting to Rs. 110 billion in 2027, to support affordability and volumes despite elevated inflation. Together with our relentless focus on cost and innovation, this gives us confidence in the momentum we carry into the second half. Above all, we will continue to Move with Courage. With a clear strategy, trusted brands and talented people, we are determined to convert this quarter’s recovery into sustained growth and lasting value for our shareholders, consumers and the communities we serve”.

title: Colombo to become communion for music, culture and peace in December | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 6 November 2026 00:20

What happens when different traditions, diverse stories, transformative ideas, cross-cultural conversations and intergenerational hope come together on shared platforms?

This December, Colombo will host a cultural gathering that seeks to answer that question through the universal languages of music, literature, heritage and human connection.

The Festival of Sacred Sounds of South Asia and Friends 2026, presented by Mindful Collective Expressions (MCE) – The Arts Collective, will take place from 1–7 December 2026, bringing together acclaimed artists, musicians, writers, poets, scholars and cultural practitioners from across South Asia and beyond. Cargills is the Festival’s Principal Sponsor.

Under the theme “Beyond Differences Towards a Deeper Understanding of Shared Humanity,” the Festival seeks to create a space in which cultural diversity becomes a source of connection and artistic expression, opening pathways to discussion, exploration and celebration of shares human values across traditions.

Representatives from SAARC member countries — Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka — alongside international friends, including participants from Iran, Poland and the United Arab Emirates, will transform Colombo into a meeting ground for the exchange of cultures, ideas and artistic traditions.

This is not simply a series of performances. It is an invitation to encounter one another differently — through the music we inherit, the stories we tell, the histories we share and the futures we have the power to shape together.

With Cargills as Principal Sponsor, the Festival marks an important milestone in the continuing work of Mindful Collective Expressions to advance artistic collaboration, intercultural understanding and peacebuilding through the arts.

As preparations gather momentum, MCE is mobilising additional financial resources, institutional partnerships and in-kind contributions to realise the full ambition of this seven-day regional and international gathering.

The Festival presents an opportunity for corporate institutions, philanthropic foundations, cultural organisations and individual benefactors to become part of a wider cultural undertaking — one that supports artists, creates meaningful opportunities for young people, strengthens regional connections and places the arts at the heart of conversation that awaken understanding and solidarity.

MCE welcomes partners who share this vision to join the initiative and contribute to building a Festival whose impact extends beyond its December program. The ambition is not only to bring people together in Colombo, but to establish relationships, collaborations and cultural exchanges that can continue to grow across borders long after the Festival concludes.

At a time when the need for understanding across communities remains profound, the Festival advances a compelling proposition: that our differences need not divide us, and that artistic expression can help us discover the humanity we hold in common.

title: JAT Holdings ups revenue by 36% to Rs. 7 b in 1H led by foreign operations | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 6 November 2026 00:04
-     - 41

JAT Holdings PLC has recorded Group revenue of Rs. 7.01 billion for the six months ended 30 September 2026, representing a 36% year-on-year increase, supported by growth across its local businesses and a higher contribution from international operations.

Local revenue increased by 14% to Rs. 4.56 billion, primarily supported by the emulsion category, while foreign operations revenue increased by 115% to Rs. 2.45 billion, reflecting improving business conditions in Bangladesh and JAT’s expanding international presence. Gross profit margin across foreign markets also improved from 24% to 26% during the period, reflecting the growing contribution of international operations to both the scale and profitability of the Group.

Gross profit increased by 36% to Rs. 2.46 billion, maintaining a 35% gross profit margin despite higher raw material import costs and rising fuel prices. Operating profit increased by 15% to Rs. 653 million, while operating margin moderated from 11% to 9% amid higher administrative, selling and distribution expenses associated with consolidation of Mirotone operation, Volt software amortisation, transportation and expanded storage capacity. Favourable exchange rate movements helped reduce finance costs, with profit before tax increasing by 27% to Rs. 602 million and profit after tax rising by 27% to Rs. 504 million.

CEO Nishal Ferdinando said: “Our first-half performance reflects the increasing breadth of the Group’s growth, with stronger contributions from both our local businesses and international operations, including continued growth across our industrial and retail businesses in Bangladesh. Maintaining our gross profit margin amid higher input costs also reinforces the value of the investments we have made in manufacturing efficiency and backward vertical integration. As we move into the second half, our focus remains on translating this broader operating base into sustained profitability and long-term growth.”

JAT’s wood coatings business expanded its market share to 57.1%, recording 2% revenue growth and a 1.6% improvement in net gross profit margin, supported by efficiencies gained through the second phase of its Acrylic Binder Plant upgrade. Its loyalty customer base grew by 7% to exceed 191,000, contributing approximately 78% to 80% of sales.

The decorative paints segment recorded 107% revenue growth, supported by strong performance across key brands including White by JAT, Hydro Plus and Wallz, while gross profit margin across the segment improved by 1.4%. The segment also expanded its innovation portfolio with the introduction of JAT HeatBlock20 to the industrial market. Brushes and Rollers retained market leadership with a 31% market share and 11% revenue growth. 

The furnishing business also recorded 16% growth, supported by a confirmed project pipeline of Rs. 561 million. Together, these results reflect continued growth beyond JAT’s traditional wood coatings base, strengthening the Group’s increasingly diversified revenue portfolio.

JAT continued to deepen its manufacturing integration across Sri Lanka and Bangladesh during the period. The upgraded Acrylic Binder Plant in Sri Lanka, together with the commencement of alkyd resin exports from Bangladesh to Sri Lanka, further strengthened the Group’s backward vertical integration, supporting greater manufacturing control and a more resilient regional supply platform.

Volt Charge continued to expand its technology capabilities during the period, invoicing 2,000 L2 chargers to John Keells CG Auto for BYD vehicles, completing engineering of a 200 kW commercial vehicle charger and increasing its Volt app user base to 25,000 active users. While revenue declined by 5% due to the timing of revenue recognition, these developments reflected continued progress in scaling both its hardware and digital charging ecosystem.  The business also commenced a pilot project for electric two- and three-wheeler charging, with the first charger installed in Kottawa.

Internationally, Bangladesh recorded 26% industrial sales growth, 42% retail sales growth and a 151% increase in CoatEX revenue, demonstrating broader-based growth across JAT’s established industrial business and its expanding retail presence.  

Mirotone New Zealand recorded month-on-month sales growth of 12% in August and 9% in September, indicating improving momentum following slower sales movement in Q1. The business reported a first-half loss of NZD 99,000 amid challenging market conditions. Initial sales to Fiji were also recorded during the period, marking an early step in expanding Mirotone’s export reach from New Zealand.

Mirotone Australia continued to advance its market re-entry, with its local facility and colour-matching infrastructure now fully established. Product R&D and market testing progressed during the period, while initial shipments supported product familiarisation and commercial discussions.

Managing Director Aelian Gunawardene said: “The progress we are seeing across Bangladesh, New Zealand and Australia reflects the increasing scale and reach of JAT’s international platform. Alongside the continued development of newer business verticals, this is creating a more diversified Group with multiple avenues for growth. Our long-term ambition remains to build a stronger Sri Lankan multinational with the capabilities and market presence to compete sustainably across regional and international markets.”

title: Sri Lanka’s CH17 takes proprietary SaaS technology beyond borders with Nepal expansion | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 6 November 2026 00:02
-     - 27

CH17 Founder and CEO Jumar Preena (right) with CH17 Systems Ltd., Nepal Co-Founder Vivek Thakuri

Sri Lankan loyalty and customer engagement technology company CH17 has taken a significant step towards international expansion with the establishment of Channel17 Systems Ltd., in Nepal, marking its first overseas market operation under its own brand.

The development represents more than geographical expansion. It opens a new avenue for international recognition of Sri Lankan-developed proprietary Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) technology, particularly in the specialised fields of loyalty management, customer intelligence, digital engagement and customer value-added services.

Established in 2013, CH17 has spent more than a decade developing technology-driven solutions for organisations across Sri Lanka’s insurance, finance and leasing, apparel and retail industries.

Its experience has evolved into a proprietary technology ecosystem that enables businesses to introduce customised loyalty, rewards, membership management and customer engagement programmes under their own corporate identities.

CH17’s international ambitions are supported by practical experience in developing and managing white-label technology solutions for established organisations operating across diverse industries.

A distinguishing feature of its business model is its pioneering focus on closed and targeted customer communities, identified through demographic, firmographic and institutional relationships.

This approach enables organisations to engage specific customer groups more effectively, moving beyond conventional mass-market promotions towards relevant, measurable and sustained customer relationships.

CH17’s proprietary SaaS infrastructure supports digital membership identification, customer authentication, loyalty and rewards management, customer segmentation, promotional campaign administration, merchant privileges and customer intelligence reporting.

The technology is designed to accommodate different institutional requirements while allowing participating organisations to retain their individual brand identities.

Beyond technology development, CH17 has established expertise in introducing innovative, out-of-the-box marketing and customer engagement strategies to industries traditionally dependent on product-led promotions, conventional advertising and transactional customer relationships.

As customer expectations evolve, businesses increasingly require solutions that extend engagement beyond the initial sale, policy issuance, financial transaction or membership enrolment.

CH17 addresses this requirement by combining technology with practical marketing intelligence, structured customer recognition, year-round privileges and measurable engagement opportunities.

Its approach is particularly relevant to insurance, finance and leasing, and other established industries seeking to modernise customer relationships without necessarily replacing their existing core business systems.

The company’s proprietary solutions allow businesses to develop more meaningful customer relationships, encourage participation, strengthen retention strategies and create additional value through external merchant partnerships.

CH17’s technological and commercial capabilities have progressively evolved into its Customer Value as a Service (C-VAAS) framework.

The model integrates three complementary disciplines: technology infrastructure, customer intelligence and customer engagement.

However, the company’s proprietary SaaS capabilities extend beyond conventional loyalty programmes and customer value-added services.

Its technology architecture also offers applications in white-label membership management, digital verification, rewards exchange, institutional engagement, customer segmentation and campaign management.

This versatility creates opportunities for CH17’s technology to be deployed across multiple sectors and international markets, with configurations tailored to local business requirements.

The company’s approach combines Human Intelligence supported by Artificial Intelligence, recognising that effective customer engagement requires both technological capability and practical understanding of customer behaviour.

The establishment of Channel17 Systems Ltd., in Nepal on 30 October 2026 marks the beginning of CH17’s international market development strategy.

The Nepal operation has been established with local business partners to pursue opportunities across retail, financial services, insurance and other customer-oriented industries.

Under the proposed operating structure, the Nepal entity will focus on local business development, client relationships and market operations, while CH17’s Colombo operation will provide proprietary technology, platform licensing, technical support and agreed specialist services.

This asset-light operating model is intended to create opportunities for recurring technology and service export revenue originating from Sri Lanka.

Importantly, the expansion demonstrates how locally developed intellectual property can be introduced to overseas markets without the need to rebuild technology platforms for each country.

It also provides a potential foundation for evaluating further international market opportunities through suitably qualified local partners.

CH17 Founder and CEO Jumar Preena said: “Sri Lanka has established a strong reputation for software development and technology services. We believe the next opportunity lies in gaining international recognition for proprietary technology platforms, intellectual property and innovative business solutions developed within Sri Lanka.

Over the past thirteen years, we have gained valuable experience in understanding the customer engagement challenges faced by established industries. We have translated that experience into proprietary, white-label technology solutions supported by practical marketing intelligence.”

“Our entry into Nepal is not simply about taking a loyalty programme overseas. It is about introducing Sri Lankan-developed technology, specialised industry knowledge and innovative customer engagement solutions to international markets. We believe Sri Lanka has the expertise and intellectual capacity to create technology products that can be commercially deployed beyond our shores under our own brands. Our objective is to demonstrate that potential through sustainable international business development.”

CH17’s international expansion reflects a broader ambition to position Sri Lankan-developed SaaS solutions within the global marketplace for customer engagement and business technology.

With its proprietary technology platform, experience across multiple industries and focus on scalable white-label solutions, the company aims to establish a sustainable international presence while retaining its technology development and intellectual property base in Sri Lanka.

For Sri Lanka, it offers another example of how homegrown technology, industry expertise and innovative thinking can create opportunities for international recognition and technology exports.

title: Connect to Care strengthens platform for regional philanthropic partnerships and Global South impact | Daily FT

Connect to Care (CTC) has reached two significant institutional milestones with its NGO registration and an Equivalency Determination (ED) on file with NGOsource, strengthening its foundation for philanthropic partnerships and its ability to support development priorities in Sri Lanka and across the wider region.

Connect to Care Consulting’s Equivalency Determination recognises the organisation as equivalent to a US public charity for international grant-making purposes and remains valid until 31 March 2028. Together with its NGO registration, the milestone provides CTC with a stronger institutional platform to engage philanthropic organisations, development partners, governments and technical experts around programs designed to deliver sustainable impact.

These developments represent an important step for CTC in its broader ambition to serve as a neutral platform for collaboration, connecting local knowledge and institutional experience with global expertise, philanthropy and implementation capabilities.

Chairman Chandita Samaranayake said: “These milestones strengthen the institutional foundation from which Connect to Care can build meaningful partnerships in Sri Lanka and across the region. Our role is to bring together organisations and individuals with complementary capabilities around development priorities where collaboration can create lasting value. We want to provide a credible platform through which local experience, global expertise and philanthropic support can come together around shared outcomes.”

CTC works alongside Government, philanthropic and development partners across areas including digital transformation, Digital Public Infrastructure, agriculture, healthcare, nutrition and sustainable development. Its approach is centred on strengthening existing institutional systems and bringing together the capabilities required to move programs from strategy to implementation.

The Equivalency Determination is expected to further support CTC’s engagement with US-based philanthropic organisations by simplifying an important aspect of the international grant-making process for participating foundations. This creates a clearer pathway for CTC to develop partnerships that can support locally grounded programs while connecting them with international expertise and resources.

The milestone also comes as CTC strengthens its focus beyond Sri Lanka, with an emerging regional presence across South and Southeast Asia. title: The anti-establishment paradox: What America’s midterm revolt reveals about Sri Lanka’s NPP | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 6 November 2026 00:26
-     - 38

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake with US President Donald Trump during the special dinner reception hosted by the latter at the Lotte New York Palace Hotel, for the heads of state who had arrived in New York to participate in the 80th Session of the United Nations General Assembly in September 2025

From Washington to Colombo, movements elected to overturn the political establishment face a fundamental contradiction: the powers they once condemned become the instruments through which they govern. Their lasting significance depends not simply on how they exercise authority, but on whether they are willing to constrain it

Political movements rarely discover the deepest contradictions of their revolutions while fighting for power. Those contradictions emerge after victory, when the institutions they promised to transform become the instruments through which they govern. The electorate united by rejection of the old establishment begins to divide over what should replace it, while political authority once condemned as excessive becomes increasingly convenient to those who inherit it. The defining challenge of an anti-establishment Government is therefore not merely retaining public support, but overcoming the institutional incentives that can turn yesterday’s reformers into custodians of the system they opposed.

America’s November 2026 midterm elections expose the fragility of political mandates built around dissatisfaction. Democrats have secured control of both chambers of Congress, overturning Republican dominance through victories extending into traditionally conservative states, including Texas, Kansas and South Carolina. Two years after Donald Trump’s return to the White House, voters have fundamentally altered the balance of political power in Washington. Frustration over living costs, the war with Iran and presidential authority contributed to the reversal. Yet its significance extends beyond Trump’s political fortunes. It demonstrates how electoral coalitions assembled around dissatisfaction can weaken when governing exposes the competing expectations beneath them.

For Sri Lanka, the comparison raises a more consequential question. President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s National People’s Power (NPP) Government emerged from the economic catastrophe of 2022 promising not merely different political leadership, but a transformation of the structures associated with corruption, impunity and economic mismanagement. Its historic mandate represented a profound rejection of conventional politics. Two years later, the challenge is whether that rejection can produce enduring institutional change, or whether the practical demands of governing will gradually reconcile reformers to the powers they once sought to dismantle.

Trump and Dissanayake are not ideological equivalents. One leads a conservative nationalist movement in the world’s largest economy; the other heads a left-leaning coalition governing a heavily indebted developing state. Their circumstances and constitutional systems differ fundamentally. What connects them is a structural dilemma: anti-establishment movements can acquire extraordinary electoral authority without acquiring an equally coherent mandate over how that authority should be exercised.

The electoral mandate that conceals its contradictions

The NPP’s November 2024 parliamentary victory transformed Sri Lanka’s political landscape. Having secured just three seats in 2020, it won 159 of Parliament’s 225 seats four years later, attracting 6.86 million votes and 61.56% of valid ballots. Yet the scale of this victory concealed the diversity of the electorate behind it. Economically distressed households, professionals demanding competent administration, younger voters seeking opportunity and citizens determined to prevent the return of political figures associated with the crisis converged around a common rejection of the established order.

Their agreement about what had failed did not necessarily constitute agreement about what should follow. Fiscal consolidation, taxation, public-sector reform and redistribution impose different burdens on different constituencies. Electoral movements can unite voters by postponing these disagreements; Governments must eventually confront them.

This distinction between a negative electoral consensus and a positive governing settlement explains an important vulnerability of anti-establishment politics. The former identifies what voters collectively reject; the latter requires Governments to reconcile competing interests. Political scientist V.O. Key’s work on retrospective voting provides a useful framework: citizens assess incumbents partly through their experience of Government rather than their initial ideological commitments. Once elected, reformist movements gradually lose the ability to define themselves through their predecessors’ failures.


Sri Lanka’s May 2025 local elections illustrated the conditional nature of electoral support. The NPP remained the leading political force, securing 4,503,930 votes and 43.26% of valid ballots, compared with 61.56% in the preceding parliamentary election. Differences in turnout, candidates and electoral incentives prevent the results from being treated as a direct measure of declining national support. Nevertheless, the extraordinary parliamentary coalition was not automatically reproducible.

America’s midterms reveal a related mechanism. Trump’s 2024 coalition combined committed ideological supporters with voters motivated by inflation, immigration and dissatisfaction with the previous administration. The Democratic advance does not establish a permanent ideological realignment. It demonstrates that coalitions formed through shared grievances remain vulnerable when governing outcomes fail to reconcile competing expectations.

When economic recovery fails to restore political confidence

Economic conditions expose these contradictions with particular force. A Reuters/Ipsos survey conducted immediately before the American midterms found that 48% of registered voters identified living costs as their principal electoral concern, compared with 26% citing democratic norms and 13% immigration. Nearly half reported that their household finances had deteriorated since Trump’s return. Even amid disputes concerning presidential authority and foreign policy, material insecurity remained central to electoral judgment.

Sri Lanka faces a different but equally revealing problem. The World Bank’s October 2026 Sri Lanka Development Update reports economic growth of 4.7% during the first half of the year, with real GDP returning to pre-crisis levels. Growth is projected at 4.4% for 2026, reflecting macroeconomic stabilisation, fiscal consolidation and recovering economic activity. These are consequential achievements following the sovereign default and economic dislocation of 2022.

Yet the same assessment estimates poverty at 16.9% in 2025, substantially above pre-crisis levels. Household incomes and labour-market conditions have recovered more slowly than aggregate output, while renewed inflationary pressures have weakened purchasing power.

This produces a recovery–legitimacy gap: the distance between improvements Governments demonstrate statistically and progress citizens experience materially. Governments measure recovery through growth, fiscal performance and debt sustainability; households experience it through wages, prices, employment and financial security. Both assessments can be accurate simultaneously, but political legitimacy increasingly depends on whether aggregate recovery translates into visible improvements in daily life.

Verité Research’s July 2026 Mood of the Nation survey illustrates this divergence. Government approval stood at approximately 50%, down from 65% in February. The proportion believing economic conditions were improving fell from 64% to 42%, while 56% described current conditions as poor. These findings do not establish an inevitable electoral trajectory, but demonstrate that macroeconomic improvement need not produce equivalent political confidence.

The NPP inherited exceptional fiscal constraints, and abandoning stabilisation for immediate popularity could undermine recovery itself. Nevertheless, economic inheritance cannot indefinitely determine political accountability. As Governments remain in office, citizens increasingly judge them through present conditions rather than the failures of previous administrations. Stabilisation may restore financial credibility; durable legitimacy requires productive employment, rising real incomes and economic opportunity.

The institutional inheritance trap

The deeper contradiction concerns political authority itself. Anti-establishment movements gain legitimacy by condemning executive overreach, political privilege and institutions vulnerable to manipulation. Once elected, they inherit those same constitutional and administrative powers. Authority previously portrayed as an obstacle to democracy becomes a convenient instrument for implementing the Government’s program.

This is the institutional inheritance trap: Governments elected to constrain political power may discover that retaining inherited authority makes governing easier than reforming it.


The mechanism is not necessarily personal hypocrisy. It is an institutional incentive. Centralised authority can accelerate decisions, reduce bargaining costs and facilitate reforms that fragmented institutions might obstruct. Governments confronting economic crises may reasonably conclude that dismantling executive powers before establishing viable alternatives could generate instability.

Yet this creates a dilemma. If concentrated authority is continually justified by the need to complete reforms, the promised transformation can become dependent on preserving precisely the powers it was intended to restrict. Temporary necessity risks evolving into permanent political convenience.

Sri Lanka’s executive presidency illustrates this tension. The NPP’s 2024 manifesto promised a new constitution and abolition of the executive presidential system. The Government has reaffirmed that commitment, with Prime Minister Harini Amarasuriya explaining that constitutional reform requires examining existing proposals, developing a new constitutional framework and undertaking public consultation. Nevertheless, abolition remains unrealised, and a definitive timetable has not been publicly established.

In September 2026, Parliament passed the 22nd Amendment by 158 votes to 63, increasing the retirement ages of Supreme Court and Court of Appeal judges and expanding the latter court. The amendment demonstrated the Government’s capacity to advance constitutional legislation, although it did not address the abolition of executive presidential authority.

Constitutional transformation undeniably requires careful design, including decisions concerning parliamentary stability, devolution and electoral representation. Delay does not itself establish abandoned intentions. The relevant distinction is whether postponement is accompanied by a credible process, transparent milestones and meaningful public scrutiny, or whether continued possession of executive authority gradually becomes an end in itself.

The NPP’s record also resists simplistic declarations of institutional failure. The Proceeds of Crime Act, amendments to the National Audit Act and repeal of statutory entitlements for former presidents represent concrete reforms. Their enduring significance, however, depends on consistent enforcement and institutions capable of holding officeholders accountable irrespective of political affiliation.

Counterterrorism legislation presents a more contested test. The Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill, gazetted in September 2026 as a proposed replacement for the Prevention of Terrorism Act, contains certain procedural improvements. However, the Centre for Policy Alternatives has argued that provisions involving executive detention, broad definitions and restrictions on fundamental freedoms risk perpetuating weaknesses of the previous framework.

The disagreement concerns whether legislative reform meaningfully constrains coercive authority or merely modifies the procedures through which inherited powers operate. Changing officeholders alters who possesses authority; transforming institutions determines how that authority can be exercised, challenged and restrained.

Why America’s constitutional system changes the calculation

The American comparison becomes most instructive through the differences between the two constitutional systems.

The United States allows voters to redistribute legislative authority without removing the president. Democratic control of Congress will constrain aspects of Trump’s legislative agenda and strengthen opportunities for congressional oversight when the newly elected Congress convenes in January 2027. The president retains substantial executive authority, including veto powers, but must operate alongside a separately elected legislature controlled by political opponents.


Sri Lanka possesses no equivalent nationwide congressional midterm mechanism. Its presidential and parliamentary mandates operate through different electoral arrangements, making judicial independence, parliamentary scrutiny, autonomous commissions and public auditing particularly important between national elections.

Neither arrangement guarantees accountability. Divided Government can produce legislative paralysis, while concentrated parliamentary authority can facilitate necessary reforms. The distinction is that the two constitutional systems distribute incentives for institutional restraint differently.

In America, an electoral reversal can introduce additional checks on executive power during a presidential term. In Sri Lanka, where the NPP commands a two-thirds parliamentary majority, the Government’s capacity to implement reform is accompanied by greater responsibility for establishing safeguards that restrain its own authority.

This produces the article’s central constitutional paradox: the parliamentary strength that makes systemic reform achievable can simultaneously reduce the political pressure to undertake it. The more effectively a governing coalition consolidates authority, the less immediately necessary institutional self-restraint may appear.

The distinction is therefore between reforms Governments can implement because they possess concentrated power and reforms that prevent future Governments from exercising that power arbitrarily. The former strengthens governing capacity; the latter strengthens the constitutional order.

The danger of political dissatisfaction without an alternative

A further difference concerns Opposition politics. America’s two-party competition provided dissatisfied voters with an established electoral vehicle capable of assuming congressional control. Sri Lanka’s opposition remains fragmented, with prominent parties carrying associations with previous administrations and facing difficulties establishing a convincing alternative program.

Consequently, dissatisfaction with the Government need not translate into support for its opponents. Where citizens remain unconvinced by available alternatives, disillusionment may instead manifest through abstention, political disengagement or declining confidence in representative institutions.

This matters particularly for the NPP because its original mandate emerged from a broader crisis of confidence in conventional politics. If expectations of institutional transformation remain unmet, the consequences could extend beyond one administration’s popularity to public confidence in democratic change itself.

The real test of political transformation

America’s midterms do not predict Sri Lanka’s political future. The countries possess fundamentally different political institutions, and the NPP retains substantial public support alongside identifiable economic and legislative achievements. The comparison instead illuminates a broader democratic problem: movements elected through rejection must eventually convert that rejection into a governing settlement capable of surviving changes in political leadership.

For Sri Lanka, economic recovery and institutional transformation are inseparable. Recovery without enforceable accountability risks preserving vulnerabilities associated with previous failures, while constitutional reform without improvements in livelihoods risks disappointing citizens whose demands for political change emerged from economic insecurity.

The lasting significance of the NPP’s mandate should therefore be measured through more than electoral dominance, economic indicators or the personal integrity of present officeholders. It depends on whether institutional safeguards become sufficiently independent to restrain Governments that may not share the reformist commitments of those who established them.


The fundamental contradiction confronting anti-establishment Governments is that electoral victory transfers the very powers reformers once condemned. Their most enduring achievement would be to establish a political order in which accountability no longer depends on the character or intentions of those exercising authority.

Sri Lanka’s transformation will ultimately be measured not by how decisively the NPP displaced the previous establishment, but by how much less power any future establishment will be able to abuse.

(The author is an International Relations student at Monash University whose writing explores politics, governance, and international affairs)
