PROF. Senaka Bandaranayake, in the preface to his book 'The

University of the Future,' wrote this opening line: To the researcher and the academic in the developing world, the eagerness to contribute to institution and nation building, in whatever modest a way, often becomes almost as exciting and challenging as the dedication to study, investigation, experiment and discovery. 

I understand the value of that write-up, having been part of the national university system for over four decades. I may say we sacrificed a lot of potential research time to the former trying and crying. The University of the Future is yet to come, and our engagement with the nation and for the nation is still tenuous at best! Another statement I remember is a line from the address to the Malaysian Academy of Sciences by Prof Douglas Osheroff – 1996 Nobel Laureate in Physics. I saw the liquid doing something unusual; that told me right away that some sort of ordering was going on in the liquid, and I wrote it in my lab book that night. It was 2.40 in the morning, by the way. I had discovered the BCS transition in liquid helium-3. That was how it was done. This research was done in a highly supportive environment, though it may not have been obvious at the time. An open lab at 2.40 a.m. The researcher’s freedom is understood, and given all the support, not the nation but the world changes.

An event on a day in a Month in 2026. It wasn’t exactly exciting when you got a call from your Head of the Department saying the ‘audit’ was right here with her, asking for a piece of equipment bought around 2013 and wanting to confirm that the exact piece is there, recorded in the books, and present in the lab. I knew about the instrument because we were interested in vehicle fuel consumption, and these were level gauges and associated components. The audit interest was because the purchase was made with public money, and the sole purpose was to verify that the physical assets were still present. The next couple of hours were spent on telephone calls, running around to find the lab owners (the researcher really has no ownership of the lab), and ensuring that, before one leaves, what needs to be seen is shown. I should say that was done, and whether that time and energy elevated the institution to a new level, I am sure it did not. Now that tells a story and is definitely food for thought on why we make no progress. Let me elaborate more on that. The story is exciting, though in reality quite depressing.

We never check, nor are we interested in, the return on investment of public money for research. If the assets and final report are present, and an evaluation report has been duly filed with some boxes appropriately ticked, that is identified, reported, and concluded as research completed and money spent and accounted for. In this manner, whether you spend 0.1% of your GDP on R&D or 2% of GDP on R&D is irrelevant. The State has no plan for the output, so meaningful outcomes never arise. Since no one sees tangible economic benefits, no one tries to allocate more rupees to research. An unproductive annual cycle of standard allocation and substandard progress continues. The administration is engaged in a meaningless pursuit of verification.


When the call came, the auditors were in the building, waiting to be taken to show the public-financed assets; one had to move fast, too. When I received the call, I was at a different meeting outside. The assets in question were related to a project funded in 2013 or thereabouts. The research student is now happily and productively based in Australia, having been invited from Sri Lanka on a PhD scholarship (funded by an Australian university through grant money from a Foundation in the USA). The decision to award the scholarship came after a half-hour Skype (yes, at the time the only VOIP system in use) call the student had with the Australian research group. Because of his master’s work (again supervised by me and in the department) and ongoing research, he had the knowledge and computational skills to fill a gap that existed in the research team in Australia. My next step was to call Australia immediately and, fortunately, I connected, as the research student who completed an equipment handover to the lab before departing quickly. Fortunately, Earth’s rotation kept my research student up at the time, down under. If audits don’t find what they’re looking for, they file an observation, and I must spend a good portion of my time writing explanations, since their filings are sacred. Of course, the auditors were genuinely doing their assigned duty. My grouse is that they should do this task differently. They should assess what outputs materialised and whether the knowledge created moved to the next level. Essentially, they should check for a decent ROI on the knowledge assets created through research funding and help overcome obstacles to realising that ROI. This does not happen – our audit mindset is in apprehending rogues, and all are presumed in that category unless shown otherwise. I blame leadership for not understanding this and for failing to transform the audit process into one of development enablement. Again, the lesson to be taken is why results were not made use of – we were looking at life cycle assessments of biofuels both technically and socially. Whatever skills we developed, I am sure Australia used them quite profitably. We bake the cake for someone to savor the taste. That is why I say the current auditing method should change to address issues and find solutions for researchers. Researchers in Sri Lanka face many issues today, and at times you wonder why you want to do research. Times have changed, but the issues have just scaled up.

An interesting fact about this piece of instrumentation is that it had to be fixed into the vehicle’s fuel tank, which means it would be moving out of the laboratory to which the asset has been allocated. The system refused to fix the unit to a vehicle, as the custodian is worried about an item moving outside the laboratory and not being returned to the cupboard. With such a unit, the piece of equipment will not return to a
cupboard. Of course, he worried that when he retires, his retirement benefits will not be available because of a mismatch in the asset list. Believe you get how the story ended – this part of the research never happened. You also learn why researchers are ready to depart at the drop of a hat. George Bernard Shaw once remarked on the Ceylonese originality. Time has passed since then. Today, the creative spirit has been siphoned off. We keep working, keeping an accounting of each cent of the King’s money (I use the term King’s money because the Audit process is a relic of those times) without really understanding the value and intended function of an investment in research. Our audit must embrace development auditing – seeing why the intended result did not happen and seeking rectification of such to ensure that the next expenditure has more chances of productive delivery.

(The author is Senior Professor in Chemical and Process Engineering, Department of Chemical and Process Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, University of Moratuwa)

title: Why should people have to adapt to technology? | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 6 November 2026 00:23
-     - 21

After years of illness and rehabilitation, Sri Lankan author Mohamed 

Rihazudin Razik is using his experiences to rethink how technology should work for people

We use technology almost every day. We read messages, fill in forms, make payments, attend meetings and look for information online.

For many people, these are simple tasks. We hardly give them a second thought.

But not everyone finds them easy.

A person with poor eyesight may struggle to read a website. Someone with unsteady hands may find it difficult to use a mouse or a touchscreen. An older person may become confused by an application that has too many instructions. A student may need more time to read and understand a passage.

We often expect people to find a way around these difficulties.

I have come to believe that we should be asking a different question.

Why can't technology make things easier for the person using it? a question that came from experience.

I was 22 when I was diagnosed with a brain tumour.

Over the years, I underwent seven surgeries, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and a long period of rehabilitation.

There were things I had once done without thinking that became difficult. My balance was affected. Writing became a challenge. Reading and concentrating sometimes required more effort than before.

I had to learn to approach many ordinary activities differently.

I also came to understand how frustrating it can be when something that appears simple to another person becomes difficult for you.

Sometimes I needed help. At other times, I wanted the opportunity to try for myself, even if it took longer.

That distinction mattered to me.

I did not always want someone to do things for me. I wanted to be able to do as much as possible on my own.

These experiences stayed with me as I continued learning and working with technology.

Technology should understand the person

Today, we have software that can carry out complicated tasks in seconds. We can communicate across countries, attend classes from home and access information that once required a visit to a library.

Yet something as ordinary as reading a page on a screen can still be difficult for many people.

We tend to design systems around how we expect people to use them. When someone struggles, we may assume that the person needs more training or practice.

Sometimes that is true.

But sometimes the problem lies in the design itself.

A website with small text, confusing instructions or too many steps can create difficulties that need not exist.

I began thinking about what might happen if we approached technology from the other direction.

Instead of expecting every person to use a system in the same way, could we give people more choice in how they use it?

That thinking helped shape Rihazudin i³ — Idea · Innovate · Implement.

Starting with reading

One of the projects I have been working on is an accessible digital reading platform.

The idea grew partly from my own difficulties with reading and concentrating.

I wanted to explore whether a reader could adjust the way information appeared on a screen rather than having to accept a fixed layout.

The platform is being developed with options such as changing text size, adjusting colours, focusing on smaller sections of text and listening to written content.

Some of these features are already available in the working demonstration. Others are still being developed and tested.

I do not believe that one setting will suit everyone.

A person with dyslexia may prefer a different reading layout. Someone with visual difficulty may need larger text or stronger contrast. Another reader may simply find it easier to listen.

Even the same person may need different settings on different days.

My intention is to give readers more control over their experience.

Beyond the reading platform

The idea behind Rihazudin i³ is not limited to reading.

I am interested in how technology can make everyday activities easier in education, healthcare, workplaces and small businesses.

For example, an employee recovering from an illness may need a different way to interact with a computer. A student may understand a lesson better when information is presented in more than one format. An older person may benefit from a digital service that uses clearer instructions.

These are not necessarily problems that require complicated inventions.

Sometimes a small change in the way something works can make a considerable difference.

I am also interested in how organisations can make better use of technology without creating unnecessary complexity or waste.

There is still much to learn, test and improve. I would rather develop something useful and demonstrate what it can do than make promises that have not yet been proven.

The connection with my memoir

My memoir, 'If You Hug Me, I Will Fall', tells the story of my illness, the people who helped me and the years I spent trying to regain my independence.

The title reflects something I learnt during rehabilitation.

There were times when I needed someone beside me, but not necessarily someone holding me up.

If I was to improve my balance, I needed the chance to stand and try, even when I was unsteady.

That experience has influenced how I think about technology.

Good support should not take away a person’s independence. Where possible, it should help them do more for themselves.

I see a connection between that lesson and the work I am trying to do through Rihazudin i³.

An invitation to INFOTEL 2026

From 6 to 8 November 2026, I will be taking part in INFOTEL at BMICH, Colombo. Visitors can find Rihazudin i³ in Hall B, Stall 20.

I will be sharing the ideas behind the initiative, introducing the accessible reading platform and discussing how similar approaches might be useful in other areas.

I would particularly welcome conversations with educators, healthcare professionals, software developers, businesses and people who have experienced difficulties using digital services.

Their experiences and suggestions can help shape what comes next.

I am not presenting Rihazudin i³ as the answer to every problem. It is a beginning, built on personal experience, continued learning and the belief that we can make technology more considerate of the people using it.

After everything I have experienced, one thing has become clear to me.

People do not all move, read, learn or work in the same way.

There is no reason why technology should expect them to.

(The author is Founder, Rihazudin i³ and author of ‘If You Hug Me, I Will Fall’ and can be reached via email at rihazr@gmail.com or by visiting www.rihazudini3.com.lk)

title: 2027 Budget should strengthen external sector capacity | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 6 November 2026 00:22
-     - 18

The Government is expected to present its Budget for the year 2027 on 12 November. This is going to be a totally different Budget, even though the Government is required to stick to certain IMF guidelines. The dynamics of the economy have changed in 2026. The Treasury has excessive savings. On the contrary, the external sector will be experiencing a deficit in 2026 and in 2027, according to IMF forecasts.

Accordingly, I think this raises an important macroeconomic policy question: Should fiscal policy be determined primarily by the Government’s revenue position, or should it also respond to the country’s external-sector capacity?

How much additional Government expenditure can the economy accommodate without creating an unsustainable balance-of-payments problem?

The next Budget should be able to answer the above macroeconomic questions. The answer would require developing a fiscal expenditure framework strengthening the external sector. Or this Budget would present an External-Sector-Compatible Fiscal Expenditure Framework.

This does not mean that Sri Lanka can’t increase Government expenditure even when the external sector is experiencing a deficit. It is also true that a Government Budget surplus is not a guarantee of a current account surplus, and a Government Budget deficit does not automatically produce a current account deficit.

My view is that these two phenomena should be examined separately.

Understanding Sri Lanka’s present position

According to the IMF’s May 2026 review (Country Report No. 26/111), actual economic performance is as follows.

Like a doctor checks all vitals of a patient, economists check the vitals of the economy. As per the above chart vitals for the year 2025 were good. But the IMF projects a current account deficit of $534 million for 2026. If the deficit continues in 2027 the external position would come under pressure. One reason could be higher fuel import costs. But it is only one reason. Higher private credit growth than expected could also be another significant reason. Increasing Government expenditure without targeting to strengthen the external sector can create heavy pressure on external accounts.

Why increasing Government expenditure can create external pressure

Consider the following transmission mechanism. The Government increases expenditure. As a result, household disposable income and business revenue increase. And if there is no proper monetary policy or administrative control to contain private credit growth, the demand for imported goods increases, almost exponentially, creating pressure on the external sector.

Also, suppose the Government increases expenditure while commercial banks simultaneously expand private-sector credit.

Both activities can increase aggregate domestic demand.

If the private credit expansion finances vehicle imports, consumer goods and other imports, the external-sector pressure could become substantial.

Therefore, fiscal expansion should be coordinated with monetary and credit policy.

The objective should not simply be to increase or decrease money supply. It should be to ensure that additional purchasing power is accompanied by an appropriate expansion of domestic productive capacity.

However, not all Government expenditure produces the same external-sector consequences, if the Government is careful as to what expenditure should increase.

What type of Government expenditure should increase?

Basically, we can think of three strategic scenarios.

Scenario 1 – Immediate economic recovery

Scenario 2 – Import reduction

Scenario 3 – Foreign exchange generation

The ultimate objective should be to transform Sri Lanka from an economy primarily dependent on importing industrial technology into an economy that participates in producing the technologies of the AI era, while addressing the challenges of immediate economic recovery. The above three scenarios are formulated for that purpose. For example, I am hopeful that if Sri Lanka thinks of developing solid-state battery production technology, not only will we be self-sufficient in energy production (stabilising the national grid), but also, we will export solid-state batteries to neighbouring countries. If the Government takes the lead, there are capable Sri Lankan entrepreneurs who can venture into such futuristic technological areas.

The Government should evaluate each strategic expenditure scenario mentioned above and select major expenditure programs according to its expected foreign exchange consequences.

A new approach

I would suggest introducing an expenditure policy based on increasing external-sector capacity.

The Government should not unnecessarily suppress productive Government expenditure merely to maintain an exceptionally high primary surplus when the external-sector constraints can be addressed through expenditure composition. The IMF itself recognised the need for fiscal easing in 2026 in response to economic shocks, while requiring a return to a 2.3% primary surplus from 2027 onwards.

However, there is one important qualification in following the said approach. The Government must also consider interest payments, debt-service obligations and the availability of sustainable financing. The primary surplus alone does not measure the Government’s complete fiscal capacity.

Such a framework could help Sri Lanka determine the appropriate level of Government expenditure in its Budget by examining its effects on domestic production, imports, exports, private credit and foreign exchange reserves.

title: The capital order and the political economy of PSTA and POCA | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 6 November 2026 00:21
-     - 56

A public protest against the proposed PSTA and POCA

The National People’s Power (NPP) Government has Gazetted two Bills ostensibly intended to replace the Prevention of Terrorism (Temporary) Act (PTA), enacted in 1978—nearly five decades ago—despite the word temporary in its title. The repeal of the PTA has long been regarded by local and international human rights and democratic activists as imperative for the establishment of democratic governance and the rule of law. Nevertheless, successive Governments since 1978 have refused to repeal it. Moreover, the PTA has been extensively deployed to suppress and oppress political opponents. The NPP Government, which came to power promising to repeal the Act, has itself resorted to its provisions over the past two years to harass potential political opponents.

The Government has now taken steps to fulfil its promise of repealing the PTA, only to propose replacing it with two equally if not more draconian pieces of legislation: the Protection of the State from Terrorism Act (PSTA) and the Prevention of Organised Crime Act (POCA).

These two Bills would provide the Government with greater coercive powers under the guise of protecting the state and preventing organised crime. Lawyers, democratic and human rights activists, and international organisations have demonstrated in considerable detail how the enactment of these bills would undermine citizens’ rights. The focus of this note, however, is not on their legal ramifications. Rather, it seeks to examine their political-economic dimensions.

Political economy posits that understanding a phenomenon requires situating it within its broader social, economic, and political context. What explains the NPP Government’s decision to introduce a new set of draconian laws despite its electoral promise to abolish such existing legislation? Could the Government continue to function without these laws? Or is their enactment intrinsically connected to the Government’s broader socioeconomic policies? This article seeks to examine these and other related questions.

Towards the concentration of power

In the current discourse, two principal, though closely related, explanations have emerged.

The first explanation draws on a foundational concept in the social sciences: the self-reinforcing feedback loop. This concept suggests that once an individual or collective acquires power, it also gains access to resources and institutional mechanisms that can be mobilised to accumulate still more power. Hence, the familiar saying that “power begets power.”

The Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna (JVP), the core political force within the NPP, was established approximately six decades ago. For the first time in its history, it has acquired the opportunity to exercise state power and control and manage resources and Governmental mechanisms that have long been affected by multiple forms of corruption. Historical experience, particularly in the Global South, provides ample evidence of the concentration of power and resources in the hands of a small political elite.

The second explanation relates the proposed legislation to the ideological history of the JVP. Proponents of this view argue that the JVP’s ideological orientation essentially favours a totalitarian or authoritarian state, drawing inspiration from models associated with either Hitler or Stalin. According to this interpretation, the proposed legislation reflects an essentially undemocratic political project aimed at defending the regime rather than merely enriching particular individuals or groups. Nevertheless, the distinction between a model of individual or group enrichment and one of regime preservation is not fundamental. As international experience demonstrates, the transition from one to the other can be relatively easy.


In defending the Government’s intentions, NPP leaders repeatedly emphasise that their Government has so far refrained from using excessive force in dealing with protests and demonstrations against it. They therefore present the proposed legislation as essentially precautionary measures rather than instruments intended for immediate use. However, two fundamental features must be present in any counterterrorism legislation if it is to possess legal and moral legitimacy.

First, the legislation must be clear and precise, leaving little room for arbitrary interpretation or misuse. Yet the definition of terrorism in the proposed legislation is excessively broad.

Second, counterterrorism legislation must incorporate effective safeguards for freedom of expression, peaceful assembly, association, religion or belief, and participation in public affairs. Any restrictions on these rights must be lawful, necessary, and proportionate to a legitimate objective.

The two proposed bills appear to fail these tests. As international human rights organisations have demonstrated, the PSTA, together with the POCA, seeks to impose “unjustified restrictions on freedoms of expression, including media freedom, peaceful assembly and association, despite the new safeguards in sections 3 (4), 8 (2), 10 (3) and 11.”

The former Chief Justice, former and incumbent presidents of the Bar Association of Sri Lanka, and other distinguished legal professionals have also pointed out that many provisions of the proposed legislation are imprecise and excessively broad. Such provisions could potentially allow even routine and innocent media reporting to be categorised as an act of terrorism.

Austerity and authoritarianism

The Italian political economist Clara E. Mattei has drawn attention to the nexus between the concentration of political power and the imposition of austerity policies. In 2017, Mattei first developed this argument in her article, “Austerity and Repressive Politics: Italian Economists in the Early Years of the Fascist Government,” published in The European Journal of the History of Economic Thought. She subsequently elaborated on the argument in her book The Capital Order: How Economists Invented Austerity and Paved the Way to Fascism.

Mattei’s central argument is that austerity is not merely a technical economic policy but also a political instrument for protecting capitalism and suppressing working-class challenges to the existing social order. To preserve and protect what she calls the capital order, painful measures must be imposed, supported by carefully designed instruments of political power.

For example, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe has reportedly argued that the “correct” policies should have been adopted even if they ran counter to the wishes of the people. This position resonates with the views expressed by former Chair of the US Federal Reserve System Jerome Powell. Powell argued that, in order to “restore price stability,” economic policymakers must use their instruments “forcefully,” acknowledging that doing so “will also bring some pain.” The pain, in this formulation, is to be borne by those held responsible for inflation, particularly those who are consuming too much and working too little.

The former Chair of the US Federal Reserve and the present CBSL Governor, thus appear to articulate a similar position: corrective economic measures must be implemented even when they impose considerable hardship on the population.

But what happens when such measures encounter resistance? If opposition emerges from the lower strata of society, the necessary political and institutional precautions must be taken to ensure their implementation.

Authoritarian political power can facilitate the implementation of austerity by suppressing resistance from workers and other popular groups. Mattei argues that, “in the Italian case, Fascism and austerity reinforced one another: Fascism provided the coercive political conditions for austerity, while austerity helped restore capitalist social relations”.

According to Mattei, repressive legislation, an empowered executive, and a subservient judiciary are not necessarily isolated institutional developments. They can form part of a broader political project directed towards the implementation of austerity policies, including cuts in public expenditure on health and education, reductions in social security, and the dismantling of the remaining institutions of the social welfare order.

From this perspective, the proposed PSTA and POCA should not be examined solely as counterterrorism or crime-prevention measures. They must also be situated within the broader political economy of the NPP Government’s economic program designed, developed and backed by the International Monetary Fund.

The critical question, therefore, is whether the concentration of coercive power and the implementation of austerity are mutually reinforcing processes in contemporary Sri Lanka, as Mattei’s historical analysis suggests. If so, the proposed legislation may represent not merely an attempt to strengthen the State’s capacity to maintain law and order, but also an effort to establish the political conditions necessary for restructuring the existing social order in favour of capital.

(The author is a retired teacher in economics and could be reached via email  sumanasiri.liyanage@gmail.com)

title: 2027 Budget: From economic recovery to prosperity – what the nation should expect | Daily FT
summary:

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake

The 12 November Budget must go beyond fiscal consolidation and revenue collection to deliver meaningful relief to households, strengthen businesses, stimulate investment and translate economic recovery into 

sustainable prosperity

Introduction: A Budget at a critical economic crossroads

Sri Lanka’s 2027 Budget arrives at a pivotal stage of economic recovery. Since the 2022 crisis, the country has restored macroeconomic stability, strengthened public finances and resumed growth. However, recovery remains incomplete, with households and businesses continuing to face financial pressures. Presented on 12 November, 2026, the Budget 2027 offers an opportunity to move beyond fiscal stabilisation towards inclusive growth, employment, productivity and improved living standards.

The challenge is to transform economic recovery into tangible prosperity for the nation.

What exactly is a National Budget?

A national Budget is the Government’s annual financial and economic policy statement, outlining revenue, expenditure, borrowing and development priorities. It reflects the Government’s economic direction and commitment to national development. Through taxation, public spending, subsidies and investment, the Budget directly affects individuals, businesses and the wider economy—shaping living costs, public services, investment, employment and economic growth. Ultimately, a Budget’s success should be measured not merely by revenue collection or fiscal surpluses, but by its ability to transform public resources into tangible economic and social benefits.

Why the 2027 Budget is particularly important

Sri Lanka’s present circumstances demand a careful balance between economic discipline and public welfare.

1. Completing the economic recovery

According to the World Bank’s October 2026 Sri Lanka Development Update, the economy grew by 4.7% in the first half of 2026, with projected growth of 4.4% in 2026 and 4.2% in 2027. Although real GDP has returned to pre-crisis levels, poverty remains elevated, labour-market recovery is incomplete and household welfare improvements remain uneven. Budget 2027 must therefore move beyond macroeconomic stabilisation to strengthen sustainable growth, employment generation and inclusive economic development.

2. Addressing the cost of living

Despite improved economic stability, households continue to face financial pressures from food, transport, electricity, healthcare, education and housing costs. The cumulative impact of the economic crisis and fiscal adjustments has weakened purchasing power. Budget 2027 should therefore prioritise household affordability, improved public services and targeted social protection while maintaining fiscal sustainability.

3. Supporting business recovery and investment

Businesses continue to face higher taxation, compliance costs, financing constraints and operational uncertainties. Private-sector investment is vital for employment, exports, innovation and productivity. Budget 2027 should therefore promote a predictable, business-friendly environment that encourages investment, expansion, technological advancement and sustainable economic growth.

4. Maintaining fiscal discipline and debt sustainability

Sri Lanka’s recovery remains closely linked to its IMF-supported program and debt restructuring commitments. Maintaining fiscal discipline, strengthening revenue mobilisation and ensuring sustainable expenditure are essential. However, excessive taxation without improved public expenditure efficiency could weaken consumption, investment and public confidence. Budget 2027 must therefore balance fiscal responsibility with inclusive economic growth and improved public welfare.

What has the Government achieved through previous Budgets?

The Government’s fiscal performance during 2025 provides an important foundation for assessing the expectations surrounding Budget 2027.

Significant improvement in public finances

According to the IMF’s 2026 program review, Sri Lanka recorded the following fiscal outcomes in 2025:

The primary surplus reached 5.4% of GDP, significantly exceeding the 2.3% program target, while revenue and grants rose to 16.7% against the projected 14.7%. These achievements reflect improved fiscal management and revenue mobilisation (IMF, Sri Lanka Fifth and Sixth Reviews under the Extended Fund Facility, 2026).

Revenue mobilisation through taxation

Government revenue improved through economic recovery, stronger tax compliance and increased motor vehicle imports in 2025, which contributed approximately 2.8% of GDP in revenue, according to the IMF. However, this exceptional revenue reflects pent-up demand following import restrictions and may not be sustainable. Budget 2027 must therefore strengthen long-term revenue sustainability through broader tax compliance, economic expansion and a more productive tax base, rather than excessive reliance on exceptional or consumption-driven taxation.

Strengthening tax administration

The Government has continued modernising tax administration through expanded taxpayer registration, improved compliance and digital revenue collection. RAMIS 2.0 and enhanced VAT compliance are important developments. However, their effectiveness depends on efficient implementation, taxpayer accessibility and improved service delivery. Budget 2027 should further strengthen a transparent, efficient and taxpayer-friendly system that encourages voluntary compliance, economic activity and public confidence.

Budget 2027: What tax changes could we expect?

Taxation will be a key focus of Budget 2027, with households and businesses expecting tax relief, greater policy predictability and improved administration. However, significant tax reductions must be balanced against revenue requirements, debt sustainability and IMF commitments. The challenge is to introduce reforms that support economic activity and household welfare while preserving fiscal stability. The following areas deserve particular attention:

1. Personal Income Tax: Relief for employees and professionals

Personal income taxation remains an important concern for employees, professionals, consultants and self-employed individuals. Possible policy discussions may include:

A carefully designed revision of personal income tax could improve disposable income and encourage greater formal economic participation. However, the extent of any revision will depend on the Government’s revenue position and the policy commitments announced in the Budget.

2. Corporate Income Tax: Encouraging investment and enterprise development

Corporate taxation is particularly important for businesses operating in manufacturing, exports, tourism, technology, agriculture and professional services. Businesses require a predictable tax environment in which investment decisions can be made with confidence. Potential areas for consideration include:

Targeted tax incentives could stimulate investment, employment and taxable economic activity. Rather than granting indiscriminate concessions, the Government should consider incentives linked to measurable outcomes such as job creation, export growth, technological advancement and regional development.

3. VAT: Will consumers and businesses receive relief?

Value Added Tax (VAT), currently imposed at 18%, remains a major indirect tax affecting consumers and businesses. It influences consumer prices, business costs and working capital requirements. Budget 2027 is expected to address the following key VAT-related issues:

Any VAT rate reduction must be carefully assessed against its fiscal impact, as broad reductions could cause significant revenue losses. Targeted relief on essential goods and services, improved VAT refunds and simplified administration may offer a more sustainable alternative. For businesses, timely refunds, predictable administration, simplified filing and lower compliance costs could provide greater benefits than a general rate reduction.

4. Social Security Contribution Levy (SSCL): A major business concern

The Social Security Contribution Levy (SSCL), imposed at 2.5% on applicable turnover, represents a significant indirect tax burden on businesses. As it is generally based on turnover rather than profit, businesses operating on narrow margins may face considerable pressure, particularly across multiple stages of commercial activity. Budget 2027 could therefore consider:

A reduction or rationalisation of SSCL could improve business cash flow and competitiveness. Nevertheless, any substantial reduction would require careful consideration of revenue implications and the need to avoid creating further distortions within the taxation system.

5. Tax exemptions and concessions: A more targeted approach

Tax exemptions and concessions can promote economic development when properly designed. However, indiscriminate concessions may reduce revenue, create tax inequities and weaken the tax system. Budget 2027 offers an opportunity to review existing exemptions and establish a transparent, targeted framework focused on measurable economic and social benefits. Potential priorities include:

The emphasis should be on concessions that produce measurable economic benefits rather than exemptions granted without clear performance objectives.

The SME sector: The most important opportunity for Budget reform

Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are vital to Sri Lanka’s employment, domestic production, services and regional economic activity. However, they often face high compliance costs, limited access to finance, administrative complexity and competitive disadvantages. Budget 2027 could introduce a comprehensive SME support framework addressing:

An important consideration is the distinction between providing genuine assistance to small businesses and creating tax structures that encourage businesses to remain artificially below registration thresholds. The objective should be to encourage SMEs to grow, formalise and become more productive.

Beyond taxation: What should the Budget deliver to the general public?

The public’s expectations extend well beyond tax concessions.

Cost-of-living relief

The Budget should examine the affordability of essential goods and services and the efficiency of existing social support mechanisms. Targeted support for low-income households, vulnerable groups and economically disadvantaged communities would be more sustainable than poorly targeted subsidies.

Healthcare and education

Adequate allocations for healthcare, education and public infrastructure are essential for long-term development. The Government should prioritise improvements in service quality, accessibility and efficiency rather than focusing exclusively on increasing expenditure.

Employment and income generation

Sri Lanka requires employment opportunities that provide sustainable incomes and improve household economic security. The Budget should encourage private-sector investment, vocational training, entrepreneurship and productive employment opportunities.

Agriculture and food security

Agriculture remains essential for livelihoods, food security and rural development. Investment in irrigation, agricultural technology, storage facilities, value addition, logistics and market access could reduce wastage and improve farmer incomes.

Housing and infrastructure

Affordable housing, transport infrastructure, urban development and regional connectivity are important components of inclusive growth. Well-designed infrastructure investment can create employment while improving the productive capacity of the economy.

One of Sri Lanka’s oldest sporting traditions returns this November as the Mercantile Rugby Football Association (MRFA) hosts the 54th Mercantile Rugby Sevens on 13 and 14 November 2026 at the CR & FC Grounds.

First played in 1966, when Shaw Wallace & Hedges Ltd lifted the inaugural title, the Mercantile Rugby Sevens has spanned six decades and 54 editions, making it one of the longest-running corporate tournaments in the country. Over the years it has grown from a contest among a handful of trading houses into a celebration of speed, skill, camaraderie and sportsmanship across the entire corporate sector, with generations of players going on to represent leading clubs and the national side.

The tournament’s roll of honour reads like a history of Sri Lankan business. John Keells stands as the most successful institution in the event’s history, with eleven titles, beginning with a hat-trick from 1968 to 1970 and most recently winning as John Keells Holdings PLC in 2022 and 2024. Hatton National Bank follows closely with nine championships, including its own hat-trick from 1991 to 1993 and back-to-back wins in 2001 and 2002. The modern era has been shaped by MAS Holdings, whose seven titles include three in a row from 2013 to 2015 and a shared crown with Access Group in 2019.

Other famous names have also left their mark. Brown and Co., Ceylon Tobacco, Butani Exports, Asia Capital, Sampath Bank, Seylan Bank and Emjay International each claimed consecutive titles in their time, while Aitken Spence, A. Baur and Co., Jade Gardens Sports Club, Nation Lanka Finance and 3DH International have all etched their names on the trophy. Link Natural arrive at the 2026 edition as defending champions after claiming the title in 2025, and will be looking to join the select group of teams to have successfully defended their crown.

Teams will compete across Four tiers suited to their strength and experience. The Cup and Plate is an open competition with no limit on registered club players. The Bowl allows up to four registered club players in a squad, with no more than three on the field at any time. The Shield allows up to two registered club players, with only one permitted on the field at any time. This structure gives companies of every size and rugby background a fair and competitive pathway into the tournament.

The MRFA invites rugby fans, families and colleagues to keep 13 and 14 November free. Entrance to all matches at the CR & FC Grounds will be free of charge, offering spectators two full days of fast-paced sevens rugby and the chance to cheer on their teams in a vibrant weekend atmosphere. Further details on the tournament, including rules and eligibility, are available on the MRFA website at www.mrfa.lk.

Sri Lanka will host the 12th Asian and Oceanian Championship of the International Optimist Dinghy Association (IODA) from 12 to 19 December at Port City Colombo, bringing together young sailors from across the world for one of the region’s major international Optimist sailing championships.

With 20 countries registered and 130 boats expected on the water, the championship will feature individual and team racing across three fleets in the under-15 Optimist class, one of the world’s largest youth sailing classes.

Sailors from Asian and Oceanic countries as well Argentina, Brazil, the Czech Republic, France and the USA will compete in this year’s championship.

“Hosting the IODA Asian and Oceanian Championship is a significant milestone for Sri Lankan sailing. It will provide our young sailors the opportunity to compete against some of the best in the region,” said Lalin Jirasinha, President of the Yachting Association of Sri Lanka (YASL).

Racing will be held over five days, with clear skies and average winds of 8-12 knots expected.

“With three continental titles and an overall Asian and Oceanian title at stake, the championship offers competitors more than a single overall podium,” said Sarath Kuragama, Chief Operating Officer of YASL.

Last year, Thailand took the individual overall title, Singapore won the Team Racing Championship and the USA claimed the Nations Cup.

Individual prizes will go to the top three competitors overall, the top three girls, and the top three sailors from Asia and Oceania respectively. Titles will also be awarded to the leading Asian and Oceanian girls and boys, and the Overall Asian and Oceanian Champion.

In team racing, prizes will be awarded to the top three teams overall, the leading Asian and Oceanian teams, and the best-placed team from either continent, which will receive the IODA Perpetual Trophy and the Asian & Oceanian Team Racing title.

Around 60 foreign coaches, team leaders, managers and other officials will join the sailors alongside international jury members. Renowned Turkish International Sailing Judge and International Race Officer Ilker Byindir will serve as Principal Race Officer, while Malaysian veteran sailor and coach Mohamed Afendy will serve as the race officer.

“As one of the most prestigious events on the IODA calendar for the Asia and Oceania region, the championship brings together the continent’s top young sailors to compete at the highest level of the class,” said Captain Ajay Kumar Narang (Retd), IODA Vice President - Africa, Asia and Oceania.

“The 2026 Optimist Asian & Oceanian Championship marks an exciting return to Sri Lanka, a nation with a proud sailing tradition and a proven record of hosting outstanding international Optimist competition,” he added.

Sri Lanka last hosted the championship in 2016 in Trincomalee, following an earlier edition in 2012. The country was awarded the 2020 championship, but it was cancelled due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

The island has also hosted several international sailing events, including the South Asian Yachting Regatta from 1970 to 1978 and again in 2004, the Enterprise World Championships in 2006 and the GP14 World Championships in 2011.

The event, organised by YASL in collaboration with the Ministry of Sports, IODA and other local stakeholders, “will boost sports tourism and strengthen Sri Lanka’s position as a destination for international sailing,” said Jirasinha.

“We also hope it will encourage the development of sailing programs in the country, especially in the North and East,” he said.

The championship is supported by the Sri Lanka Tourism Promotion Bureau, the Ministry of Defence, and Port City Colombo, while One Plus Boat Co. Ltd. of China will provide charter boats to the competitors. Kingsbury Hotel will accommodate all sailors and teams.

The Sri Lanka Navy, which has assisted with previous international sailing events, will provide rescue services and shore facilities.

The championship has grown into a major competition for young Optimist sailors across Asia and Oceania. Last year’s edition in Oman attracted more than 180 sailors from 25 countries.
